questions.explanation: charAt returns the character at the given zero-based index; index 1 of '594' is '9'. Index zero would be the first digit, not the second. The printed value is 9, while the alternatives come from reading index zero instead of one, reading the final digit and choosing the next digit instead.
questions.hint: String positions start counting at zero.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving strings — slice.

answer.exemplar: With one argument, slice returns everything from that index to the end, dropping the first character of '595'. The result is '95'. The result is 95.

questions.explanation: With one argument, slice returns everything from that index to the end, dropping the first character of '595'. The result is '95'. A complete answer names 95 and justifies it from the code rather than guessing.
questions.hint: A single slice index means from there to the end.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving strings — split join.

options.misconception: Counting a separator after the last digit
Dropping a digit from the count

questions.explanation: split turns '596' into 3 characters and join inserts a dash between each pair, giving 5 characters. There are one fewer separators than digits. The printed value is 5, while the alternatives come from ignoring the inserted separators, counting a separator after the last digit and dropping a digit from the count.
questions.hint: Count the dashes between digits, not after the last one.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving objects — access.
questions.explanation: Bracket access with the exact key string retrieves 597, and adding one gives 598. A mistyped key would produce undefined, not zero. Both the direct number 598 and the equivalent sum 299 plus 299 match, whereas 597 and 599 come from forgetting the addition of one and adding two by mistake.
questions.hint: Bracket notation uses the key name as a string.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving objects — keys.

options.misconception: Assuming only the first property is enumerable
Counting entries as if values were keys

questions.explanation: Object.keys returns the enumerable own property names, which are a, b and c, so its length is three. Values such as 598 do not affect the count. The printed value is 3, while the alternatives come from counting only numeric-looking keys, counting entries as if values were keys and assuming only the first property is enumerable.
questions.hint: keys returns names, not the stored values.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving objects — destructuring.
questions.explanation: Destructuring binds a to 599 and b to 7 by matching property names, so their sum is 606. Order in the pattern does not matter for objects. Carrying the operation through gives 606; common slips include using only the first destructured field and using only the second field.
questions.hint: Object destructuring matches by property name.
